title: The Bereans (Acts 17:1–15)
hook: they received the word eagerly and searched the scriptures daily to check
tomorrow: Paul in Athens finds an altar with no name on it…

segments.voice: At midnight they sang, feet in the stocks, before anything had changed. Now Paul and Silas leave Philippi and walk on, to cities that will test every word they say.
screen: `AT MIDNIGHT THEY SANG.` → `CITIES THAT TEST EVERY WORD.`

segments.voice: A clip goes around claiming a famous verse means something wild. The comments pile up, and somewhere one person quietly opens the actual book. No hot take, no reply, just a finger on the page. Acts has a name for people like that. In Thessalonica, Paul reasons in the synagogue "as his manner was." Some are persuaded; others stir up a crowd that shouts these men "have turned the world upside down," and the believers send Paul and Silas away by night, to Berea. And there, Acts stops the story to praise the listeners. So who checks a preacher's homework? The Bereans.
screen: `ONE PERSON OPENS THE BOOK.` → `SENT AWAY BY NIGHT.` → `WHO CHECKS THE HOMEWORK?`

segments.voice: Here's the praise: "These were more noble than those in Thessalonica, in that they received the word with all readiness of mind, and searched the scriptures daily, whether those things were so." Two halves, held together. All readiness of mind: open, eager, glad to hear. And searched the scriptures daily. Searching is a hands word. You turn to the place. You run a finger down the line. You go back and compare, and you come back again tomorrow. The Greek word means examining, the way a judge looks over evidence. That's the one to tell a friend tonight: in Acts, the word noble goes to the people who double-checked the apostle. Eagerness without checking can swallow anything. Checking without eagerness can turn away everything. The Bereans did both. And look who they were: a synagogue community, reading their own scriptures carefully, and praised for it in the book of Acts. Acts says many of them believed, with Greek women of standing, and men, not a few. Then trouble follows from Thessalonica, and Paul is sent on toward Athens while Silas and Timothy stay behind. What the Bereans leave behind is a habit: hear it gladly, then open the book and see whether those things are so.
screen: `ALL READINESS OF MIND.` · `SEARCHED THE SCRIPTURES DAILY.` · `NOBLE: THEY DOUBLE-CHECKED.` · `A SYNAGOGUE, PRAISED IN ACTS.` · then, large: `SEARCH DAILY.`

segments.voice: Find a book within reach, any book. Hold it and feel its weight, open it to a page, and run your finger slowly down one line, the way you'd check something that matters, and notice the paper under your fingertip. If you have a Bible, you can open it to Acts 17:11 and let your finger rest on searched the scriptures daily.
The Bereans. Listeners in Berea who heard Paul with readiness of mind, and searched the scriptures daily.
Keep this one: search daily, with an open mind and an open book. See you then.

screen: `DAY 1516 COUNTS.` → `ACTS, READ THROUGH · 30 OF 45.` → `TOMORROW: PAUL IN ATHENS FINDS AN ALTAR WITH NO NAME ON IT…`

fork.setup: a friend excitedly sends you a post that says a well-known saying comes from the Bible. you're not sure it does. what would a Berean do?
options: thank her, then look it up before passing it on.

tell her it's fake without looking anything up.
fork.reveal: readiness of mind and a daily search: be glad she cares, then check whether those things are so.

chat.meaning: Acts praises the Bereans for readiness of mind plus checking daily whether those things were so. Hear it, then check the source.

Thessalonica.meaning: a city in Macedonia where Paul taught before Berea

Berea.meaning: a town in Macedonia whose listeners Acts praises

synagogue.meaning: a Jewish house of prayer, reading and study

Silas and Timothy.meaning: Paul's companions, who stayed behind in Berea

notes: Framing: Acts 17:5 says 'the Jews which believed not' stirred the crowd in Thessalonica. The lesson says 'others stir up a crowd' and stresses that the Bereans praised in 17:11 were themselves a synagogue community. Confirm this is fair and accurate.
'Greek women of standing, and men, not a few' paraphrases 17:12 ('honourable women which were Greeks, and of men, not a few'). 'Many of them believed' is 17:12's own wording.
'The Greek word means examining, the way a judge looks over evidence': anakrino is used for judicial examination elsewhere in Acts (e.g. 4:9, 24:8). Confirm the gloss.
'Sent on toward Athens' follows 17:14-15. Confirm the compression.
The fork deliberately names no saying, so the lesson makes no claim about what is or isn't in the Bible.
